item.title: Moving from WordPress to a static site
item.description:
Moving to a static site means no longer serving every visit with PHP and MySQL, and instead serving HTML files that are already built. The content is the same and so are the addresses, but the site loads faster, has a smaller attack surface and needs almost no maintenance.

When it makes sense

WordPress makes sense when many people edit, when there are orders and user accounts. When the site only publishes — news, projects, catalogues, portfolios — the machinery is surplus and turns into permanent maintenance work.

item.title: Custom websites
item.description:
What “custom” means

It means the decisions come from the project: which pages are needed, how information is organised, how it reads on a phone and what the person editing it must be able to do. It does not mean “expensive” or “with more features”. It often means fewer things, done properly.

Most sites we see have the opposite problem: a template with twenty sections nobody fills, widgets that load for no known reason and an admin panel nobody understands. We start from a minimal base and add only what the project asks for.

item.title: Web applications
item.description:
When a website is not enough

A website informs. An application does. The difference shows when the work has to be done every week and depends on someone who knows how: member lists, votes, bookings, time tracking, registrations, inventories, permissions.

If the process exists and lives on paper, in a spreadsheet only one person understands or in a group chat, there is an application to be built.

What we build

  • Association and collective management: members, dues, registrations, self-publishing of content.
  • Votes and decisions: anonymous voting, automatic counting, minutes and history.
  • Contests and juries: entries, works, public voting limited to the room and jury voting.
  • Time and jobs: hours per project, reports, invoicing from hours.
  • Content and publishing: platforms to publish with permissions and simple workflows.

When we do not build it

  • If a free tool already exists that does the job and can be adapted, we use it.
  • If the problem is communication, not software, we say so.
  • If the decision is to automate a process nobody has defined yet, we define it first.

How we do it

1. Understand the real process

We watch how the work is done now, on paper, in spreadsheets or in chat. The application must reproduce the process that works, not the one we wish existed.

item.title: Hosting and maintenance
item.description:
What maintenance includes

  • Hosting on our own server, with HTTPS and certificates up to date.
  • Backups daily, outside the hosting server and rotated.
  • Monitoring of availability, certificate and domain.
  • Planned updates for whatever needs them, tested first.
  • Support for small changes: a paragraph, an image, a new section.
  • Periodic review of broken links, accessibility and performance.

Why “install and forget” is not enough

A static site has very few moving parts, and that is already an advantage: no database or plugins that must be updated every week. But it still depends on things it does not control: a certificate that expires, a domain that lapses, the server it lives on, an image someone deletes or a link that stops working.

item.title: Analytics and GDPR
item.description:
Analytics that do not spy

Most analytics tools do not measure the site: they build a profile of every visitor and sell it or keep it for other uses. We do the opposite: we count visits, pages and sources without identifying people, with our own counter on the same domain that cannot be blocked and needs no cookies.

What we measure and what we do not

Yes: visits, most-viewed pages, language, device, aggregated source and conversions (for example, how many people submit the form).
